title: TCP: The Field Handbook — Handshake, Sequence Numbers, Congestion Control, TIME_WAIT & Keepalive
summary: A dense, end-to-end study guide to how TCP actually works on the wire: connection setup and teardown, sequence/ack arithmetic, retransmission and windowing, the congestion control family from Reno to BBR, and the operational realities of TIME_WAIT and keepalive. Covers mechanics, tuning knobs, trade-offs, and the mistakes engineers make in production.

chapters.title: What TCP Is and Why It Exists
points: Definition: TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, byte-stream transport protocol over the unreliable, best-effort IP datagram service (RFC 793, updated by RFC 9293).
IP gives you: possible loss, duplication, reordering, corruption, and variable delay. TCP's job is to hide all five from the application.

'Byte stream' means TCP has no message boundaries: two write() calls of 100 bytes may arrive as one read() of 200, or four reads of 50. Applications must frame their own messages (length prefix or delimiter).
Connection identity is the 4-tuple: (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). Two connections may share three of four fields but never all four.

TCP provides five services: connection setup/teardown, reliable delivery (ACK + retransmit), in-order delivery (reassembly by sequence number), flow control (protect the receiver), congestion control (protect the network).

Flow control vs congestion control: flow control stops a fast sender from overrunning a slow receiver's buffer; congestion control stops senders from overrunning routers in the middle. Different problems, different windows.
Effective send window = min(receiver advertised window rwnd, sender congestion window cwnd). Whichever is smaller is your bottleneck.
TCP is full-duplex: each direction has its own independent sequence number space, window, and close.
Where TCP sits: application → TCP (ports, reliability) → IP (addressing, routing) → link (MAC, framing). Layer 4 of the OSI model.
Cost of the guarantees: head-of-line blocking, connection setup latency (1 RTT), and per-connection kernel state — the exact reasons QUIC and UDP-based protocols exist.

chapters.title: The TCP Segment Header, Field by Field
points: Header is 20 bytes minimum, up to 60 bytes with options; the Data Offset field counts header length in 32-bit words (5 = 20 bytes, 15 = 60 bytes max).
Source Port and Destination Port: 16 bits each, so 65535 max ports; ports 0-1023 are well-known/privileged.
Sequence Number (32 bits): byte offset of the first data byte in this segment within the stream.
Acknowledgment Number (32 bits): the next byte the sender of this segment expects to receive — cumulative, and valid only when the ACK flag is set.

Flags: SYN (synchronize sequence numbers), ACK (ack field valid), FIN (no more data from sender), RST (abort connection), PSH (deliver to app now, don't buffer), URG (urgent pointer valid — effectively deprecated), plus ECE/CWR for ECN and NS.
Window (16 bits): receiver's free buffer space in bytes — caps at 65535 without the Window Scale option.
Checksum (16 bits): covers header, payload, and a pseudo-header of source IP, destination IP, protocol, and length — this is how TCP detects IP-level address corruption.
Urgent Pointer: offset to urgent data; ambiguous across implementations (BSD vs RFC interpretation), avoid it.
Key options carried in SYN: MSS (Maximum Segment Size), Window Scale (shift count 0-14), SACK-Permitted, Timestamps (TSval/TSecr), and NOP/EOL for padding to 4-byte alignment.
Options negotiated in the SYN/SYN-ACK apply for the connection's lifetime — if a middlebox strips Window Scale from the SYN, you are stuck at a 64 KB window forever.
MSS is the payload size, not the packet size: typical Ethernet MSS = 1500 MTU − 20 IP − 20 TCP = 1460 bytes.
Example wire read: `Flags [S], seq 1234567, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 99 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7]` — a SYN offering SACK, timestamps, and a 128× window scale.

chapters.title: The Three-Way Handshake
points: Step 1 — SYN: client sends SYN with its Initial Sequence Number (ISN_c), plus its options (MSS, wscale, SACK-permitted, timestamps).
Step 2 — SYN-ACK: server replies with SYN carrying ISN_s and ACK = ISN_c + 1, plus its own options.
Step 3 — ACK: client sends ACK = ISN_s + 1. Connection is ESTABLISHED on the client after step 2's arrival, on the server after step 3's arrival.
SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number even though they carry no data — this is why the ack is ISN+1.

Why three ways and not two: both sides must synchronize sequence numbers and confirm the other's ISN was received; a two-way handshake cannot protect against a delayed duplicate SYN from an old connection.
Cost: one full RTT before the first byte of application data. With TLS 1.3 add 1 more RTT; TLS 1.2 adds 2.

ISN is randomized (RFC 6528: hash of the 4-tuple plus a secret, plus a clock) to defend against off-path sequence-number-guessing and blind injection attacks. Predictable ISNs were the classic Mitnick-era vulnerability.
State machine path: client CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED. Server CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RECEIVED → ESTABLISHED.

Two queues on the server: the SYN queue (half-open, SYN_RECV state, sized by `tcp_max_syn_backlog`) and the accept queue (fully established, waiting on accept(), sized by min(backlog arg, `somaxconn`)).

SYN flood attack: attacker sends SYNs with spoofed sources and never completes step 3, exhausting the SYN queue. Defense is SYN cookies (`tcp_syncookies=1`) — the server encodes state into ISN_s and keeps no queue entry until the final ACK returns.
SYN cookies cost: options that don't fit in the cookie encoding may be lost, so use them as an overload valve, not a steady state.
TCP Fast Open (TFO, RFC 7413) sends data in the SYN using a server-issued cookie, saving 1 RTT on repeat connections — but middlebox breakage and replay concerns limit deployment.
Simultaneous open: both sides send SYN at once, both transition SYN_SENT → SYN_RECEIVED → ESTABLISHED. Legal, rare, no ambiguity because both sides ack the other's SYN.

Failure modes: no listener → RST (fast 'Connection refused'); packet dropped by firewall → SYN retries with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s… roughly 130s total on Linux with `tcp_syn_retries=6`) then ETIMEDOUT.

chapters.title: Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgments
points: Sequence numbers count bytes, not packets. A segment with seq=1000 carrying 500 bytes covers bytes 1000-1499; the next segment starts at 1500.
ACK number is cumulative and means 'I have everything below this byte' — an ACK of 1500 acknowledges all bytes up to 1499, regardless of how many segments carried them.
The 32-bit sequence space wraps at ~4.29 GB. On a 10 Gbps link that wraps in ~3.4 seconds, which is why Timestamps + PAWS (Protection Against Wrapped Sequences, RFC 7323) is mandatory at high speed.
All sequence comparisons use modulo-2^32 arithmetic: 'A is before B' means (int32)(A − B) < 0, never a plain `<`.
Tools show relative sequence numbers by default (starting at 1) — Wireshark's `tcp.options.timestamp` and 'Relative sequence numbers' setting hide the raw ISN.
Duplicate ACKs: when a receiver gets an out-of-order segment, it immediately re-sends the same cumulative ACK. Three dupACKs are the loss signal for fast retransmit.

Delayed ACK: the receiver waits up to 500 ms (Linux typically ~40 ms) hoping to piggyback the ACK on outgoing data or to ack two full segments at once (RFC 1122 requires an ACK at least every 2nd segment).

SACK (Selective Acknowledgment, RFC 2018): option carries up to 3-4 blocks of received-but-noncontiguous ranges, so the sender retransmits only the true holes instead of everything after the first gap.
D-SACK (RFC 2883) reports a duplicate received segment, letting the sender learn it retransmitted unnecessarily and undo its congestion reduction.

Retransmission ambiguity (Karn's algorithm): you cannot tell if an ACK for a retransmitted segment answers the original or the retransmission, so RTT samples from retransmitted segments are discarded — unless Timestamps are on, which resolves it exactly.

Worked example — a lost middle segment: sender transmits seq 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000 (1000 bytes each); 2000 is lost. Receiver acks 2000, then 2000, then 2000, then 2000 (with SACK blocks 3000-5000). Sender sees 3 dupACKs, retransmits only 2000; the next ACK jumps straight to 5000.
RST vs FIN in the sequence space: FIN is an orderly close consuming one sequence number; RST is an abort that carries no reliable delivery guarantee and discards buffered data.

chapters.title: Retransmission, RTO, and Loss Recovery
points: Two ways to detect loss: timer expiry (RTO — slow, conservative) and duplicate ACKs / SACK (fast retransmit — fast, keeps the pipe moving).
RTT estimation (RFC 6298): SRTT = (1−α)·SRTT + α·RTT_sample with α=1/8; RTTVAR = (1−β)·RTTVAR + β·|SRTT − sample| with β=1/4; RTO = SRTT + max(G, 4·RTTVAR).
RTO floor and initial value: RFC says initial RTO = 1 s and minimum 1 s; Linux uses a 200 ms minimum (TCP_RTO_MIN) and a 120 s maximum.
Exponential backoff: every consecutive RTO doubles the timer (Karn's algorithm second half). Repeated timeouts are catastrophic for latency — a single 200 ms RTO becomes 400, 800, 1600 ms.
Fast retransmit (RFC 5681): on the 3rd duplicate ACK, retransmit the missing segment immediately without waiting for the RTO.
Fast recovery: after fast retransmit, halve cwnd rather than collapsing to 1 MSS, and inflate the window by 1 MSS per additional dupACK to keep transmitting while the hole is filled.

SACK-based recovery / RACK-TLP (RFC 8985) is the modern default in Linux: time-based loss detection using per-segment transmit times instead of dupACK counting, plus Tail Loss Probe to recover lost tail segments without a full RTO.
Tail loss is the pathological case: if the last segments of a response are lost there are no subsequent segments to trigger dupACKs, so recovery falls back to RTO — TLP exists specifically for this.
Spurious retransmissions: reordering in the network can trigger fast retransmit when nothing was lost; D-SACK plus F-RTO detect this and undo the cwnd reduction.
Retransmission is per-segment, not per-byte-range-optimal: without SACK, a single loss forces go-back-N-like behavior, retransmitting everything after the hole.

Head-of-line blocking: the receiver holds out-of-order data in its buffer but cannot deliver it to the application until the gap is filled — one lost packet stalls the whole stream, including unrelated multiplexed HTTP/2 streams.
Diagnose in the field with `ss -ti` (shows retrans, rto, rtt, cwnd) and `nstat -az | grep -i retrans` or `netstat -s | grep -i retrans`.

chapters.title: Flow Control: The Sliding Window
points: Purpose: the receiver advertises how much free buffer it has (rwnd) so the sender never overruns it. This is about the endpoint, not the network.
The sliding window has four regions: bytes sent and acked, bytes sent but unacked (in flight), bytes that may be sent now (usable window), bytes not yet sendable.
Usable window = rwnd − (bytes sent but not yet acked). When it hits zero the sender must stop.
Window Scale option (RFC 7323) multiplies the advertised window by 2^shift (shift 0-14, max window ~1 GB). Negotiated only in the SYN — both sides must offer it or it is off.
Bandwidth-delay product (BDP) = bandwidth × RTT. To saturate a 1 Gbps link at 100 ms RTT you need ~12.5 MB in flight — far past the unscaled 64 KB ceiling.
Zero-window: receiver advertises win=0 because its buffer is full (usually a slow or stalled application). Sender freezes and starts sending zero-window probes.

Zero-window probe (persist timer): sender periodically sends a 1-byte segment to elicit a window update, because a pure window-update ACK is not retransmitted and could be lost — without probes both sides would deadlock forever.

Silly Window Syndrome: receiver advertises tiny windows as the app reads a few bytes at a time, so the sender ships tiny segments with 40 bytes of header for 1 byte of data. Fixed by Clark's solution (receiver withholds the update until it can offer a full MSS or half the buffer) and by Nagle on the sender.
Nagle's algorithm: at most one small unacked segment outstanding; buffer small writes until the outstanding ACK arrives or a full MSS accumulates. Disable with `TCP_NODELAY`.

Nagle + delayed ACK interaction is the classic 40 ms latency bug: sender withholds a small final segment waiting for an ACK, receiver withholds the ACK waiting for data. Request/response protocols must set `TCP_NODELAY`.
`TCP_CORK` (Linux) is the opposite knob: hold data until a full segment forms or 200 ms passes — useful for header+body sendfile patterns.
Auto-tuning: modern Linux sizes buffers dynamically between the bounds in `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` / `tcp_wmem`; setting SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF manually disables auto-tuning and is usually a downgrade.

chapters.title: Congestion Control Fundamentals
points: Why it exists: the 1986 NSFNET congestion collapse — throughput dropped ~1000×, from 32 kbps to 40 bps, as retransmissions of already-queued packets fed the fire. Van Jacobson's 1988 algorithms are the fix.
cwnd is a sender-side state variable with no wire representation — the receiver never sees it. Only rwnd is advertised.
Actual send limit = min(cwnd, rwnd), measured in bytes in flight (SND.NXT − SND.UNA).
Slow start: cwnd begins at IW (Initial Window, 10 MSS since RFC 6928; was 1-4) and doubles every RTT — cwnd += 1 MSS per ACK. Exponential growth, badly named.
ssthresh (slow start threshold) is the boundary: cwnd < ssthresh → slow start (exponential); cwnd ≥ ssthresh → congestion avoidance (linear, cwnd += MSS²/cwnd per ACK ≈ +1 MSS per RTT).
AIMD — Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease: +1 MSS per RTT while healthy, ×0.5 on loss. AIMD provably converges to fairness among flows sharing a bottleneck; AIAD and MIMD do not.
Loss as congestion signal: classic TCP assumes packet loss means a full router queue. This assumption breaks on wireless links where loss is corruption, causing needless throughput collapse.
Three reactions to loss, in escalating severity: dupACKs → fast retransmit + fast recovery (cwnd halved); RTO timeout → cwnd back to 1 MSS and re-enter slow start; repeated RTO → exponential backoff.
The sawtooth: cwnd climbs linearly, halves on loss, climbs again. Average utilization of a single AIMD flow on a full-BDP buffer is roughly 75%.

Bufferbloat: oversized, unmanaged router buffers mean loss-based TCP fills them entirely before detecting congestion, adding seconds of queuing delay. Mitigations are AQM (CoDel, FQ-CoDel, fq_codel qdisc) and delay-based CC.
ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification, RFC 3168): routers mark the IP header CE bit instead of dropping; receiver echoes with ECE, sender responds with CWR and reduces cwnd without any loss at all.

Congestion window validation: an idle connection's cwnd is stale — Linux resets or decays it after an idle period (`tcp_slow_start_after_idle`), which is why the first burst on a reused keep-alive connection can be slow.

chapters.title: Congestion Control Algorithms Compared
points: Tahoe (1988): slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit. Any loss drops cwnd to 1 MSS. No fast recovery.
Reno: adds fast recovery — cwnd halves instead of collapsing. Recovers well from a single loss per window, poorly from multiple.
NewReno (RFC 6582): handles multiple losses in one window using partial ACKs, staying in fast recovery until all holes are filled. The reference baseline.

CUBIC (RFC 8312, Linux default since 2.6.19): window growth is a cubic function of time since the last congestion event, independent of RTT. Grows aggressively far from the last known ceiling (W_max), cautiously near it. RTT-fair, scales to high BDP.

BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time, Google): models the path instead of reacting to loss — estimates delivery rate and min RTT, paces at the estimated bottleneck rate, keeps a small queue. Great on lossy or bufferbloated paths.
BBR trade-off: BBRv1 could be unfair to CUBIC flows and could push standing queues in shallow-buffer settings; BBRv2/v3 add ECN response and loss awareness.
Vegas: delay-based — infers congestion from rising RTT before loss occurs. Low latency, but loses badly when sharing a bottleneck with loss-based flows (it backs off, they don't).
DCTCP: data-center only. Uses fine-grained ECN marking to scale the reduction to the fraction of marked packets, holding queues to a few packets. Requires switch support and a controlled environment.

Comparison rows worth memorizing — signal / fairness / best fit: Reno (loss / RTT-biased / textbook), CUBIC (loss / RTT-fair / general internet), BBR (rate+RTT model / contested / lossy long-fat pipes), Vegas (delay / starves vs loss-based / homogeneous), DCTCP (ECN / excellent / data center).
Pacing: sending a whole cwnd as a burst causes queue spikes and loss; `fq` qdisc plus internal pacing smooths transmission. BBR requires pacing to function.
Inspect and change on Linux: `sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control`, list options with `net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control`, per-socket via `setsockopt(TCP_CONGESTION, "bbr")`.

Choosing: leave CUBIC for typical server traffic; consider BBR for high-RTT, lossy, or video-delivery paths; measure with real traffic — CC choice interacts with the qdisc, AQM, and the receiver's buffers.

chapters.title: Connection Teardown and the Four-Way Close
points: Graceful close is four segments because each direction closes independently: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK.
Active closer path: ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 (sent FIN) → FIN_WAIT_2 (its FIN acked) → TIME_WAIT (peer's FIN received and acked) → CLOSED after 2×MSL.
Passive closer path: ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT (received FIN) → LAST_ACK (sent its own FIN) → CLOSED on receiving the final ACK.
Half-close: `shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)` sends FIN but keeps reading. The peer sees EOF on read yet can still send — the basis of protocols that stream a request then read a response.
Piles of CLOSE_WAIT sockets is always an application bug: the kernel got the FIN, but your code never called close(). Look for leaked file descriptors or a missing close in an error path.
Piles of FIN_WAIT_2 means the peer never sent its FIN; Linux reaps these after `tcp_fin_timeout` (default 60 s) for orphaned sockets.

RST aborts immediately: sent on data to a closed socket, on close() with SO_LINGER timeout 0, or on a connect to a port with no listener. Buffered unsent data is discarded and the peer sees ECONNRESET.
Simultaneous close: both sides send FIN concurrently, both pass through CLOSING → TIME_WAIT.
The final ACK is unreliable — nothing acknowledges it. This asymmetry is exactly why TIME_WAIT exists on the active closer.
Design rule: whoever closes first pays the TIME_WAIT cost. Architect so the client closes, not the server, when connection churn is high.

Worked trace: `Flags [F.], seq 5000, ack 9000` (client FIN) → `Flags [.], ack 5001` (server ACK) → `Flags [F.], seq 9000, ack 5001` (server FIN) → `Flags [.], ack 9001` (client final ACK, then TIME_WAIT).

chapters.title: TIME_WAIT: Why It Exists and How to Live With It
points: Definition: after the active closer sends the final ACK, the socket sits in TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime) before releasing the 4-tuple. Linux hardcodes this at 60 s (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN), not tunable via sysctl.

Reason 1 — reliably terminate the connection: if the final ACK is lost, the peer retransmits its FIN. A socket still in TIME_WAIT can re-ACK it; a fully closed socket would answer with an RST, and the peer would report an error on an otherwise clean close.
Reason 2 — let old duplicates die: a delayed segment from this incarnation of the 4-tuple must expire before the same 4-tuple is reused, or stale data could be injected into a new connection.
MSL is defined as 2 minutes by RFC 793, so 2×MSL = 4 minutes in theory; BSD and Linux use shorter practical values.
TIME_WAIT is not a leak and is not a bug. It is the protocol working. Thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets on a busy proxy is normal.

Real cost 1 — port exhaustion on the client/connecting side: outbound connections draw from `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` (~28k by default). At 500 new connections/sec with 60 s TIME_WAIT you need 30k ports — you will hit EADDRNOTAVAIL.
Real cost 2 — memory and hash-table pressure, bounded by `net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets`; exceeding it makes the kernel drop TIME_WAIT state and log 'TCP: time wait bucket table overflow'.

Correct fix, in order: use persistent/keep-alive connections and connection pooling (the real fix); make the server the closer if the client side is exhausting ports; widen `ip_local_port_range`; add source IPs or destination ports to expand the 4-tuple space.
`SO_REUSEADDR` lets a server bind a port that has connections in TIME_WAIT — this is why you set it on listening sockets and why you otherwise get 'Address already in use' on restart.
`net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1` allows reusing a TIME_WAIT socket for a new *outbound* connection when timestamps confirm safety. Safe and useful on clients; it does not help inbound.

`net.ipv4.tcp_tw_recycle` was the dangerous one: it broke connections from clients behind NAT sharing a source IP with differing timestamps. Removed from Linux in 4.12 — never enable it, never copy a blog post that recommends it.
Diagnose: `ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l`, `ss -s` for a state summary, `nstat -az TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow`.

chapters.title: TCP Keepalive
points: Problem it solves: an idle TCP connection sends nothing, so neither side can distinguish 'peer is quiet' from 'peer crashed, cable pulled, or NAT dropped the mapping'. Half-open connections leak file descriptors and memory forever.
Mechanism: after an idle period, send a probe segment with a sequence number one byte *before* the current SND.NXT (deliberately old) carrying no data; the peer must respond with an ACK.

Three knobs on Linux: `tcp_keepalive_time` (idle seconds before the first probe, default 7200 = 2 hours), `tcp_keepalive_intvl` (seconds between probes, default 75), `tcp_keepalive_probes` (unanswered probes before giving up, default 9).
Default total detection time is 7200 + 9×75 ≈ 2 hours 11 minutes — uselessly long for almost every application.
Keepalive is OFF by default per socket. Enable with `setsockopt(SO_KEEPALIVE, 1)`; the sysctls are only defaults.
Per-socket overrides (Linux): `TCP_KEEPIDLE`, `TCP_KEEPINTVL`, `TCP_KEEPCNT` — always prefer these over changing system-wide sysctls in a shared environment.

Practical setting for a service behind cloud load balancers or NAT: idle 60 s, interval 10 s, 3 probes → dead peer detected in ~90 s, and traffic keeps NAT/LB idle timers (often 60-350 s) from silently dropping the flow.
Three outcomes of a probe: ACK (peer alive, timer resets); RST (peer rebooted and has no such connection → ECONNRESET); silence for all probes (→ ETIMEDOUT).

TCP keepalive vs application-level heartbeat: keepalive is free and kernel-side but only proves the TCP stack is alive — a hung application process still answers keepalives. Heartbeats prove the app is alive but cost code and bandwidth. Use both for critical services.

`TCP_USER_TIMEOUT` is the complementary knob: it bounds how long unacknowledged *data* may remain in flight before the connection is dropped, which catches stalls that keepalive (idle-only) never triggers on.

Load balancer idle timeouts are the classic production bug: an AWS NLB/ELB silently drops a flow after its idle timeout; both endpoints think it is alive; the next write hangs until RTO exhaustion. Set keepalive idle below the LB timeout.
Inspect on a live socket: `ss -tio` shows `timer:(keepalive,...)` and the remaining time.

chapters.title: Practical Tuning, Sockets, and Observability
points: Socket options that matter: `TCP_NODELAY` (disable Nagle for request/response), `SO_KEEPALIVE` + keepalive triplet, `SO_REUSEADDR` (rebind over TIME_WAIT), `SO_REUSEPORT` (multiple processes accept on one port with kernel load balancing), `TCP_USER_TIMEOUT`, `TCP_CONGESTION`.

Backlog tuning: `listen(fd, backlog)` is capped by `net.core.somaxconn` (default raised to 4096 in modern kernels; long the notorious 128). `net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog` sizes the half-open queue separately.
Accept-queue overflow is silent by default — count it with `nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops` and set `tcp_abort_on_overflow=0` (retry) vs 1 (RST) deliberately.

Buffer sysctls: `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` and `tcp_wmem` are min/default/max triples for autotuning; `net.core.rmem_max`/`wmem_max` cap explicit setsockopt values. Raise the max for high-BDP paths, keep autotuning on.
Enable at high speed: window scaling (`tcp_window_scaling=1`), SACK (`tcp_sack=1`), timestamps (`tcp_timestamps=1`) — all default-on, but middleboxes and hardened configs sometimes disable them.

MTU and MSS: PMTU discovery relies on ICMP 'fragmentation needed'; firewalls that blackhole ICMP cause the PMTU black hole — connections establish then hang on the first large packet. Mitigate with `tcp_mtu_probing=1` or MSS clamping on the router.
Offloads change what you see: GSO/TSO/GRO/LRO mean tcpdump on the host shows 64 KB 'segments' that never existed on the wire. Capture at the switch or account for it before diagnosing MSS.

Observability toolkit — `ss -tin` (per-socket cwnd, rtt, retrans, pacing rate), `ss -s` (state totals), `nstat -az` / `netstat -s` (cumulative counters), `tcpdump -i any -nn 'tcp port 443'`, Wireshark's Statistics → TCP Stream Graphs, and `tcpretrans`/`tcpconnlat` from bcc/bpftrace.
Counters worth alerting on: TcpRetransSegs ratio, TcpExtTCPTimeouts, TcpExtListenOverflows, TcpExtTCPSynRetrans, TcpExtPruneCalled (receive buffer pressure).

Wireshark expert markers and what they mean: 'TCP Retransmission' (RTO), 'Fast Retransmission' (after dupACKs), 'Dup ACK' (gap), 'Out-Of-Order' (reordering, not loss), 'Zero Window' (receiver stalled), 'Window Full' (sender blocked by rwnd).
Never tune blind: change one sysctl, measure with the real workload, keep the before/after numbers. Most 'TCP tuning guides' on the internet are cargo-culted from 2009 kernels.
Persist tuning properly in `/etc/sysctl.d/*.conf` and container/network namespaces — sysctls are namespaced, so a host tweak may not reach your pods.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Assuming message boundaries: treating one read() as one application message. TCP is a byte stream — always frame explicitly.
Assuming a successful write() means delivery: it means the bytes reached the kernel send buffer, nothing more. Only an application-level ack proves receipt.
Assuming close() flushes: with default SO_LINGER the kernel tries to flush in the background, but a subsequent RST (or SO_LINGER 0) discards the data silently.
Setting `tcp_tw_recycle=1` because a blog said it fixes TIME_WAIT — it breaks NAT'ed clients and was removed in Linux 4.12.
Fighting TIME_WAIT instead of eliminating connection churn: the fix is connection reuse and pooling, not sysctl roulette.
Leaving keepalive at defaults and wondering why dead peers linger for two hours, or forgetting that SO_KEEPALIVE is off by default entirely.
Ignoring CLOSE_WAIT growth: it is your code failing to close sockets, not a kernel issue, and it ends in EMFILE.
Leaving Nagle on for a chatty request/response protocol and eating 40 ms delayed-ACK stalls; or disabling Nagle everywhere and shipping a storm of tiny packets.
Interpreting every retransmission as network breakage: a small retransmission rate is normal and is how TCP finds the available bandwidth.
Blaming TCP for application head-of-line blocking (e.g. HTTP/2 multiplexed over one connection) — the fix is QUIC's independent streams, not TCP tuning.
Setting SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF manually and thereby disabling receive-buffer autotuning, capping throughput on long-fat paths.
Forgetting that the 64 KB window ceiling applies when Window Scale is stripped by a middlebox — throughput mysteriously caps at 64 KB / RTT regardless of link speed.
Testing over localhost or a LAN and shipping to a 150 ms-RTT, 1%-loss path: slow start, BDP, and loss recovery only show their teeth at real latency. Emulate with `tc netem`.

chapters.title: TCP in Context: Comparisons and Trade-offs
points: TCP vs UDP — TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled, byte stream, ~20-byte header, 1-RTT setup. UDP: connectionless, unreliable, unordered, no congestion control, datagram, 8-byte header, zero setup.
Pick UDP when: you can tolerate loss but not delay (real-time voice/video/games), you need multicast or broadcast, or you are building your own transport (QUIC, DNS, QUIC-based HTTP/3).

TCP vs QUIC — QUIC runs over UDP, moves reliability and congestion control to user space, merges the transport and TLS handshakes (1-RTT, 0-RTT on resumption), gives independent streams (no cross-stream head-of-line blocking), and survives IP changes via connection IDs.
QUIC costs: higher CPU per byte (user-space, per-packet crypto), less mature offload support, and blocked or throttled UDP on some networks.

TCP vs SCTP: SCTP offers message boundaries, multi-streaming, and multi-homing — technically superior for many uses, but middlebox support killed it outside telecom signaling and WebRTC data channels.
Latency budget of a fresh HTTPS request: 1 RTT for the TCP handshake + 1 RTT for TLS 1.3 (2 for TLS 1.2) + slow start ramp. Connection reuse is the single biggest performance lever.
Throughput ceiling of a single flow ≈ window / RTT. On a 100 ms path a 64 KB window caps you at ~5 Mbps regardless of the link; this is the argument for window scaling and parallel connections.
The Mathis equation approximates loss-limited throughput ≈ MSS / (RTT × √p) — halving RTT doubles throughput, and even 0.1% loss badly hurts long paths.
Reliability trade-off in one line: TCP's ordering guarantee is exactly what creates head-of-line blocking. You cannot have both without per-stream sequencing.

Comparison row for state cost: TCP keeps per-connection kernel state on both ends and in stateful middleboxes — this is what makes connection churn expensive and what makes TIME_WAIT and port exhaustion real operational limits.
Where TCP still wins: bulk transfer, anything needing broad middlebox compatibility, kernel offload performance, and universally available tooling.

chapters.title: Summary: The TCP Mental Model
points: One-line model: TCP turns a lossy packet network into an ordered byte pipe by numbering bytes, acknowledging cumulatively, retransmitting what is missing, and continuously guessing how fast the network can go.
Setup: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, 1 RTT, ISNs randomized, options (MSS, wscale, SACK, timestamps) fixed for the connection's life at this moment.
Sequence numbers count bytes; ACKs are cumulative and mean 'next byte expected'; SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number.
Loss is detected two ways — 3 dupACKs/SACK (fast, cwnd halved) or RTO (slow, cwnd to 1 MSS and back to slow start). Modern Linux uses RACK-TLP for both.
Two independent windows: rwnd protects the receiver's buffer and rides on the wire; cwnd protects the network and lives only in the sender. You send min(cwnd, rwnd).
Congestion control is slow start (exponential) up to ssthresh, then AIMD congestion avoidance (linear up, multiplicative down). CUBIC is the default; BBR models the path instead of reacting to loss.
Teardown is four-way and independent per direction; the side that closes first sits in TIME_WAIT for 60 s on Linux, and that is correct behavior protecting the final ACK and killing old duplicates.
Keepalive is opt-in per socket and useless at defaults — set idle/interval/count below your NAT and load balancer timeouts, and pair with TCP_USER_TIMEOUT.
Diagnostic reflex: `ss -tin` for the per-socket picture (cwnd, rtt, retrans), `ss -s` for state distribution, `nstat -az` for counters, tcpdump/Wireshark for the wire truth.

Three highest-leverage production levers: reuse connections (kills handshake latency, TIME_WAIT, and port exhaustion), set TCP_NODELAY for request/response traffic, and size keepalive to your infrastructure's idle timeouts.

The recurring lesson: nearly every 'TCP problem' is either an application not closing sockets, a middlebox stripping an option, or a timeout mismatch between layers — not the TCP algorithms themselves.
